cover.alt: On the first winter evening the household works and listens in the communal room. Þórunn sits at her spinning wheel; Guðrún knits; Óli works on a bed while glancing towards Helga and her book. Manga lies on a small bed by the single lamp, with Snati nearby. Siggi stands at the passage doorway.
cover.art_brief: 24 October 1874, Hamrar in Jökuldalur. Long low turf-farm baðstofa, wooden interior and beds along both sides. One fish-oil lamp lights the room. Þórunn sits at a spinning wheel; Guðrún knits a skotthúfa beside her; Óli sits on a bed doing wool work but glances at Helga with her open book by the lamp. Bjarni sits beside afi, who holds Edda. Gamla-Manga lies on a small bed by the lamp, and Snati rests beside her. Siggi stands at the passage doorway, withdrawn. Winter darkness and rain outside. Farm ink-and-watercolour style matching Kaflar 1–5. No lettering.

introductions.how: Known summer and autumn contrasted with winter; explicit antonym gloss.
Authored cow-and-door SVG shows entering and being inside the cowshed; the cattle destination is contrasted with the house.
First-use cow sound «mö» gloss, followed by sheep/horse contrast and mee/mö sounds at s005–s006.
The next sentence explains that the household sits, works and sleeps there; the authored farmhouse plan appears later at s046 and is not counted as first-use support.
Authored labelled farmhouse plan at the first göngin shows the passage leading to the communal room.
Darkness at s025, lamp taken and lit at s026, then everyone can see; same-segment gloss repeats the result.
Before-and-after visibility: the people cannot see, Guðrún kveikir á honum, then they can see. No planned vignette counted.
The next sentence supplies the known-word explanation: household work and one person reading during the evening.
Explicit contrast: not a small farmhouse but a large splendid hall. Planned woodcut does not count.

Authored hall cutaway at s072 already shows the three seats at distinct heights. At first sæti (s076), an example gloss connects the noun to a person sitting there. The next sentence and diagram distinguish niðri, uppi, hátt uppi.
Example gloss maps the sequence from now to the next now; afi first says nothing, then Edda is with Siggi.
Explicit fljótt ↔ hægt gloss and contrast between Þórunn working and Óli looking at Helga.

Authored hall SVG at first use s072 contrasts green grass on the Hamrar turf roof with visibly yellow-gold shields on the Ásgarður hall roof; labels identify both materials. The raster woodcut remains planned.
Rain outside but people inside remain dry: the prose supplies the protective roof’s function.
Known place chunks become ordinary case grammar; actual cowshed SVG shows into versus inside.
Previously known á túnið / á túninu chunks in immediate direction/location contrast; later bed and roof locations.
Lamp stays in the room while Siggi leaves for the passage; arrow gloss shows departure.
Same-place example gloss with Þórunn and the wheel; repeated named people and pronouns locate the household.
Motion arrow towards the known barn; later Gylfi approaches the seats rather than entering them.
First-use contrast with the already introduced út; cattle enter the shed at s010.
Contrast with úti; the SVG at s008 already shows the interior position.
Known farmhouse-to-field arrow gloss, immediately anchored in Siggi going out.
Known on-the-field example in the same segment; cold outdoors contrasted with the household indoors later.
Question contrast with known hvar and the arrow into the actual drawn cowshed.
Authored spinning-wheel SVG at s029 shows the big wheel, treadle, flyer, wool tuft and thread wound on the bobbin; the sound gloss is supplementary. Planned raster is not counted.
Known-word gloss gerir skotthúfu supplies making a knitted cap. Planned hands-and-needles vignette does not count. Method remains less precise without the picture: review requested.

At s039 Helga reading wakes Snati; cause-and-effect gloss supports aloud/loudly. The spatial sense high (up) first occurs in hátt uppi at s076, with an example gloss and the three-level seat diagram already attached at s072.
Known-word first-use gloss: the place where the household sleeps. Later Manga lies on one.

grammar.title: í fjósið · í fjósinu · hjá afa
grammar.rule: Hvert fer afi? — Í göngin. · Hvar er Siggi? — Í göngunum.
grammar.note_en:
A case is a form showing a word's job in a sentence. You already know the nominative (nf., nefnifall), usually the subject, and the accusative (þf., þolfall), used for the direct objects in Kafli 5. The dative (þgf., þágufall) is new. Here it follows prepositions: little words such as í, á, hjá, frá and að. The dative constructions taught here follow prepositions, rather than verbs taking dative objects.

Hvert? means "where to?": a destination. Hvar? means "where?": a location. Í and á take the accusative when someone goes into or onto a place, and the dative when someone is there. Compare inn í fjósið (s010), "into the cowshed", with inni í fjósinu (s014), "inside the cowshed". Compare í göngin (s046, s053), "into the passage", with í göngunum (s047–s048), "in the passage"; inn í baðstofuna (s064), "into the communal living and sleeping room", with í baðstofunni (s021, s048), "in the communal room"; inn í höllina (s075), "into the hall", with í höllinni (s076), "in the hall". Gylfi … fer í Ásgarð … er … í Ásgarði (s070) means "Gylfi goes to Ásgarður … is in Ásgarður". Út á túnið (s003) means "out onto the home field"; á túninu (s004) means "on the home field". The destination, rather than movement alone, matters: someone can move about within a place.

The place expressions of Kaflar 1–5, such as á túninu ("on the home field"), í bænum ("in the farmhouse"), í gilinu ("in the ravine") and í dilkinn ("into the pen"), are now examples of ordinary grammar. They no longer have to be learned only as indivisible chunks. Í usually means "in/into" and á often "on/onto"; the noun's customary preposition still needs learning.

The definite article ("the") is attached to the noun and changes for case. The table shows actual chapter forms. Masculine singular: lampa-num in hjá lampanum (s033), "by the lamp", and rokk-num in hjá rokknum (s029), "at the spinning wheel". Feminine singular: baðstofu-nni in í baðstofunni (s021), "in the communal room"; hlöðu-nni in að hlöðunni (s016), "towards the hay barn"; höll-inni in í höllinni (s076), "in the hall". These are the dative article forms -num and -inni. Lampi changes to the dative stem lampa- before -num. Baðstofa and hlaða change their final -a to -u; after that vowel the initial i of -inni drops, giving baðstofu-nni and hlöðu-nni. After höll, the full -inni remains. Neuter singular: fjósi-nu in í fjósinu (s014), "in the cowshed", and þaki-nu in á þakinu (s072), "on the roof": the article is -nu. An indefinite noun has no article: á rúmi (s031), "on a bed". In á litlu rúmi (s034), "on a little bed", litlu agrees with the dative noun; learn this encountered adjective form without extending its whole paradigm here.

Dative plural nouns commonly end in -um. Before the dative plural article -num, the m of the noun ending -um drops, producing -unum: rúm-unum in á rúmunum (s023), "on the beds"; göng-unum in í göngunum (s047), "in the passage"; sæt-unum, in á sætunum (s077), "on the seats". Göng is plural in Icelandic even though English usually calls it a single passage. The article ending is the same for all genders in the dative plural.

Hjá, frá and að take the dative regardless of this destination/location contrast. Hjá means "by, beside, at": hjá Þórunni (s030), "beside Þórunn"; hjá afa (s032), "beside Grandad"; hjá Sigga (s054, s057), "beside Siggi". Frá lampanum (s046) is "away from the lamp", and frá Svíþjóð (s070) is "from Sweden". Að hlöðunni (s016) is "towards the hay barn"; að sætunum (s078) is "up to the seats". In particular, að is a preposition here, not an infinitive marker. Af and úr come in later chapters; til with the genitive comes later too. They are not practised here.

Names have case forms too: Þórunn → Þórunni (s030), Siggi → Sigga (s054), and Hamrar → Hömrum in á Hömrum (s072), "at Hamrar". Í Svíþjóð (s067), "in Sweden", and frá Svíþjóð (s070), "from Sweden", are both dative: the spelling does not change here. Í Eddu (s059), "in Edda", is dative; Eddu in hann tekur Eddu (s051), "he takes Edda", is accusative. A form can therefore look the same in different cases.

After prepositions the pronouns change too. Hjá henni (s035) means "beside her", Manga; hjá honum (s065) means "beside him", Grandad; hjá þeim (s078) means "by them", the seats. The pronoun follows its Icelandic noun's gender: sæti is neuter, and the dative plural is þeim. Kveikir á honum (s026) means "lights it", the lamp. The dative honum follows á, the "on" element in this expression; it is not a dative object directly governed by the verb. Here the oil lamp is lit; learn kveikir á as the expression for lighting it. Á meaning "owns" is a different word: Siggi á það (s018), "Siggi owns it", the lamb.

Finally, inn and út express direction: "in" and "out". Inni and úti express location: "inside" and "outside". Kýrnar fara inn í fjósið (s010) is "The cows go into the cowshed"; Inni í fjósinu (s014) is "Inside the cowshed". Siggi … fer út á túnið. Úti er kalt (s003) means "Siggi goes out onto the home field. It is cold outside."

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: „Nú er kvöldvaka,“ segir Guðrún, og fólkið fer inn í baðstofuna.
Í baðstofunni vinnur fólkið, og þar sefur það.
„Kýrnar eru í fjósinu, ekki í baðstofunni,“ segir Óli.
„Í göngunum er kalt, en í baðstofunni er lampi,“ segir afi.
words_with_history.note_en: Baðstofa joins bað, "bath", and stofa, "room". It originally named a room for steam bathing, rather like a sauna. By the nineteenth century it was the household’s shared room for sleeping, working and listening to reading or storytelling. The name survived the change of use.

pronunciation_note.rule: ð is a soft voiced sound, like th in English this: baðstofa, Óðinn. þ is voiceless, like th in thin: þak. Keep the two letters and sounds distinct.
